paras: The threatened lynching of Dock Wright took place at Museville, Pittsylvania County, Virginia, on February 5, 1881, when a crowd of citizens sought to lynch a Black man arrested for clubbing a white man, J. C. Arthur, to death at a justice's trial. According to the wire report from Richmond, the citizens were restrained only 'with great difficulty', and a guard of ten armed men took the prisoners to the county jail. Wright was later convicted of murder and hanged legally at Chatham on March 31, 1882.

The violence began at a warrant-trying in a justice's court at Museville on a Saturday. The wire said a Black man named 'Sam Wright' had lost his case and became abusive, while evidence at the later trial held that a white man, Mastin Adkins, and Joe Minter, Wright's grandfather, had got into a fight.

Wright, by the local accounts, ran up with a heavy stick and struck at the white men present, killing Arthur with a blow to the head, shattering the arm of Maj. W. H. Murrell and breaking or cutting the hand of Christian Kendrick. Arthur, whose skull was broken, died the next morning. The wire credited the blows to a second, unnamed Black man and quoted 'persons present' calling the assault unprovoked.

The men fled to a nearby club, the 'True Friends', which in the wire's version held an all-night session and marched through the streets with the accused beating a drum at their head. A posse of twelve armed men then arrested them without further trouble. Hearing that the club planned a rescue, the officers put the prisoners under a guard of ten men with shotguns, rifles and muskets, who brought them to the county jail. After the arrest, the Staunton Spectator's version said, it was with great difficulty that 'the enraged citizens' were kept from lynching the prisoners on the spot.

Wright's trial for the murder of Cole Arthur opened at the Pittsylvania courthouse in June 1881. Thirteen of twenty-one white veniremen were excused, one of them because, in the words of a local paper quoted by the Richmond Dispatch, 'he could not give a negro a fair and impartial trial as he could a white man'. Wright was convicted, the Supreme Court of Appeals upheld the judgment in January 1882, and the governor refused to commute the sentence.

Awaiting execution, Wright three times cut his chains and once knocked down the jailer, but never got past the jail yard. Because secret societies to which he belonged threatened a rescue, the Danville Grays guarded the hanging, which took place inside a high enclosure before officers of the court and the press. On the scaffold Wright again denied the killing, and earlier that day he had said that his half-brother killed Arthur with an iron poker.

The first report was a special telegram from Chatham to the Richmond Dispatch, headlined 'Clubbed to Death', which called Wright 'an infuriated negro' and mentioned the rescue threat but not the lynching threat; the Washington Evening Star reprinted it on February 11. A longer Associated Press dispatch from Richmond, dated February 10, carried the lynching threat across the country. The Savannah Morning News headed it 'Civil Rights in Virginia', the Lancaster Daily Intelligencer 'A Colored Man's Club', and the Washington National Republican 'A Speck of War Between Colored Villians and Euraged Whites in Virginia'.

In all of these versions the near-lynching closed the story as a passing detail, and the New-York Tribune's news summary reduced it to a man who 'narrowly escaped lynching'. Coverage in 1882 turned to the appeal and the execution, which the Savannah Morning News called 'decent, quiet and orderly'; the Dispatch printed Wright's written 'farewell to the world'.

The accounts differ on the accused's name, given as Dock in the local telegram and all court reports but as Sam in the February wire. They also differ on whether one man or two did the striking and on how the fight began, with the wire blaming a dispute with the magistrate and the trial evidence a fight between Wright's grandfather and a white man. Wright himself maintained to the end that his half-brother had killed Arthur.

reader.title: Threatened lynching of Dock Wright
bases: White citizens at Museville threatened to lynch the Black man or men arrested for killing J. C. Arthur and were held back, so the anti-Black violence was a threatened lynching that was not carried out [A3, A5, A16].

The citizens who wanted to lynch the prisoners 'on the spot' were prevented, and nobody was killed by a crowd [A5, A16]; the accused, Dock Wright, was tried, convicted and hanged by the county authorities at Chatham on March 31, 1882 [A34, A35].

The local Chatham telegram to the Richmond Dispatch [A1] and the separate Associated Press wire from Richmond [A2, A3, A16] agree that a Black man clubbed J. C. Arthur to death at a Museville trial and was taken to jail under armed guard, and the wire adds that citizens could hardly be kept from lynching.

accounts.label: Local Chatham telegram
accounts.gist: One 'infuriated negro', Dock Wright, clubbed Arthur to death, broke Murrell's arm and cut Kendrick's hand at a warrant-trying; ten armed men were needed to take him to jail because the 'True Friends' threatened a rescue. It says nothing of a lynching threat.

accounts.label: Associated Press wire from Richmond
accounts.gist: Sam Wright lost a case and became abusive; a second Black man struck the whites with a stick of wood; the two fled to the True Friends' club, which paraded with drums and resolved to resist arrest; a posse of twelve arrested them and the citizens were with difficulty kept from lynching them.

accounts.label: Trial evidence (Richmond Dispatch, June 1881)
accounts.gist: Mastin Adkins and Joe Minter were fighting when Minter's grandson Dock Wright ran up with a sourwood stick, killed Cole Arthur, who had no part in the quarrel, broke Murrill's arm, and fled, boasting to Black men on the road.

accounts.label: Dock Wright's own account
accounts.gist: On the day of his execution Wright declared his innocence and said his half-brother had killed Arthur with an iron poker.

framing.detail: The Savannah Morning News ran the wire as 'Civil Rights in Virginia: Two Negroes Murder a White Man, Beat Others, and with a Crowd of their Friends Parade the Streets', presenting the near-lynching as the natural response of citizens.

Northern and western papers reprinted the wire under 'A Colored Man's Club', 'Murder in a Court-Room' and 'Trouble With Negroes', calling the assault 'most unprovoked' and the lynching threat a matter of fact.
The Richmond Dispatch's local telegram headlined 'Clubbed to Death' and called Wright 'an infuriated negro', reporting the rescue threat but no lynching threat.
The execution reports stressed that the private hanging was 'decent, quiet and orderly' and printed Wright's denial and his written 'farewell to the world'.

conflicts.note: The local Chatham telegram and every later court and execution report use Dock; Sam comes only from the February Associated Press wire, so Dock is the better-supported name.
